Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II, EDSA cor. St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFICE OF SECRETARY DILG OPINION NO.-U—S. 2002.......- 09 May 2005 MR. BONIFACIO M. QUIROG, JR. Provincial Secretary Provincial Capitol Building Tagbilaran City Dear Mr. Quirog: This refers to your request for this Department's opinion on the authority of the Provincial Qovemor to invest funds in the form of treasury bills vis-å-vis the requisite authorization from the Sangguniang Panlalawigan. As disclosed, on 15 March 1996, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Bohol issued Resolution No. 114, s. 1996, authorizing former Qovemor Rene L. Relampagos to deposit unused/idle funds of the province under time deposit accounts and government securities. Apparently, the said Resolution above became the basis for the incumbent Governor to recently invest provincial funds by purchasing treasury bills. You have now posited the following queries, to wit: I. "Can the incumbent Governor invest funds in the form of treasury bills without the authority of the present Sangguniang PanlaZawigan? 2. Can Resolution Number 114, series of 1996, authorizing the previous Governor Rene L. Relampagos, "to deposit unused/idZe funds of the province under time deposits (sic) accounts and government securities" be used as a basis for the present administration to invest in treasury bills?" Before addressing your concems, may we apprise you of certain principles regarding the fiscal administration of local government units. Please be infonned that per Section 15 of the Local Govemment Code, a local govemment unit (I-QU) has two (2) functions, i.e., govemmental and corporate. The former refers to the authority of the LGU to exercise its powers as expressly granted by the law and those necessarily implied therefrom for the promotion of the general welfare of its inhabitants.

-2- On the other hand, the corporate powers of the LQU pertain to the latter's proprietary functions to address its economic enterprises. Just like any other private corporation engaged in business, LQUs enjoy the former's attributes, such that under Section 22 of the Local Qovemment Code, LQUs are given the following corporate powers: (1) to have continuous succession in its corporate name; (2) to sue and be sued; (3) to have and use a corporate seat; (4) to acquire reat or personat property; (5) to enter into contracts; and (6) to exercise such other powers as granted to corporations, subject to limitations provided in the Code and other laws. Ergo, if the issue would only be limited to whether or not the Local Chief Executive, as the official representative of the LOU, is allowed to invest in treasury bills, then such act of investment, which falls within the ambit of the corporate powers of the LOU, finds legal basis. However, there are other things that ought to be considered. May it be noted that while LGUs, through its Chief Executives, are empowered to enter into contracts, such execution needs to satisfy certain requirements for the validity of the contract itself, to wit: 1. 2. 3. 4. The LGU has the express, implied or inherent power to enter into such a particular contract; The contract is entered into by the proper department, board, committee, officer or agent. Unless otherwise provided by the Code, no contract may be entered into by the Locat Chief Executive on behalf of the LGU without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned; The contract must comply with certain substantive requirements, i.e., when expenditure of public funds is to be made, there must be an actual appropriation and a certificate of availability of funds; and The contract must comply with the formal requirements of written contracts, e.g. the statute of frauds (Nachura, Outline Review in Political Law, 2002 Ed., p. 493). It is not amiss to point out that investment in treasury bills involves the execution of a contract between the Investor and the Bank issuing such treasury notes. Such being the case, the Local Chief Executive, who intends to invest the local government funds in such treasury bills, needs to secure prior authorization from his/her sanggunian pursuant to the clear and categorical language of Section 22 (c) of RA 7160. Otherwise stated, without prior authorization from the sanggunian Concemed, the Local Chief Executive can not enter into such contract.

-3- We now address your concerns by responding first to the second query. The Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 114, s. 1996, is rather unequivocal in authorizing a particular individual, i.e., Qovemor Rene L. Relampagos, to undertake the aforesaid banking transactions. Such authority was not couched in general terms as to vest unto the occupant of the Office of the Governor at any given time to have a continuous authority to deposit the provincial funds under time-deposit accounts or to invest said funds in treasury bills. As stated, the authority was given to fonner Qovemor Relampagos himself and such authority is thus to be considered co.-terminous with the latter's term of office. The principle of corporate succession is, therefore, inapplicable in the case at bar. Henceforth, when Governor Relampagos ceased to occupy his office, the said Resolution- Authority became functus officio. The authority enjoyed by Qovemor Relampagos cannot be "inherited" by the new Governor. Foregoing considered, we answer your second query in the negative. In view of the above explanation, your first query is, therefore, likewise answered in the negative. The new Qovemor can not invest the provincial funds in treasury bills without a new prior sanggunian authorization since, as discussed earlier, an authorization from the sanggunian is a condition precedent for a Local Chief Executive to enter on behalf of his/her LOU, into a contract, most especially when such undertaking Involves the use of public funds. We hope to have enlightened you on the matter. Legal:87/1A cc: Director Roberto C. Abejem DILG Regional Office No. 07 Cebu City Very truly yours, ANGEL T.
